---
title: "Could you recover your research data?"
last-reviewed: "2026-08-28"
---

“Everything is in Dropbox” can mean that files are synchronised. It does not tell you which copy is authoritative, whether an accidental deletion will spread, who can access sensitive material or whether recovery has ever been tested. Data management is the set of decisions that makes the project understandable and recoverable: what exists, where it belongs, who may use it, how it is backed up and what happens when the project ends. The test is not whether the files are somewhere. It is whether the right files can be found, restored and interpreted.

## Design for recovery, not just storage

A data-management plan is a living map of research materials, authority, movement, responsibility and end state. Storage is not safe merely because it is convenient or synchronised. Backup is proven only by a successful, recorded restore.

For each data or material class, identify:

`source → collection/access → authoritative copy → transformations → working copies → access → backup → sharing → retention/disposal/archive`

If any arrow is unknown, the system is not yet controlled.

## Inventory everything that matters

Research records extend beyond the final dataset. Include:

- raw observations, recordings, images, specimens or source material;
- consent, recruitment and participant-contact records;
- keys linking identities and study IDs;
- administrative, device, platform or collaborator extracts;
- field notes, lab notebooks and analytic memos;
- instruments, protocols, scripts and configuration;
- code, environments, tests and logs;
- cleaning, coding, exclusion and derivation decisions;
- intermediate and final data states;
- figures, tables, models and reports;
- approvals, agreements, licences and correspondence; and
- metadata required to understand and reuse the records.

For each item record sensitivity, owner or custodian, authority, format, size, location, access, backup, retention and final action.

## Identify the authoritative copy

Every active record needs one location or system that the team recognises as authoritative for its current state.

An authoritative copy should have:

- an approved location;
- an accountable owner or custodian;
- access controls matched to roles;
- a visible version or change history;
- a defined backup and restore route;
- rules for local or offline working copies; and
- a handover process.

Email attachments, downloads folders, chat uploads and personal desktop copies are not a data architecture.

## Separate synchronisation, versioning and backup

- **Synchronisation** keeps copies aligned across locations or devices. It can rapidly propagate deletion, corruption or ransomware.
- **Versioning** preserves prior states and supports comparison or rollback. Its retention may be limited.
- **Backup** creates a separate recoverable copy under a defined schedule and retention policy.
- **Archive** preserves selected material for long-term access under governance and metadata conditions.

One service may provide several functions, but confirm each explicitly. Do not infer recoverability from a green sync icon.

## Design access around roles and data states

Apply least privilege: people receive the minimum access needed for the current role and period.

Separate where appropriate:

- contact and recruitment information;
- consent records;
- identity linkage keys;
- identifiable source data;
- coded or pseudonymised working data;
- de-identified release data;
- restricted contracts or partner records; and
- public code, metadata and outputs.

Maintain an access register with person, role, location, permission level, approver, start date, review date and removal evidence. Shared credentials are not role-based access.

## Use a folder structure that expresses states

A simple project may begin with:

```text
project/
  README
  admin/
  protocol/
  data/
    00_incoming/
    01_raw_read_only/
    02_interim/
    03_analysis_ready/
    04_release/
  code/
  outputs/
    figures/
    tables/
    reports/
  metadata/
  logs/
```

Do not copy this blindly. Identifiable or restricted data may need a different controlled system entirely, with only non-sensitive documentation or code in the project repository.

The structure should make it difficult to overwrite raw material or mistake a working export for an approved release.

## Name files for retrieval and interpretation

A useful pattern is:

`project_item_context_YYYY-MM-DD_status_or_version.ext`

Examples:

- `atlas_interview-guide_2026-08-28_approved-v3.docx`
- `atlas_device-export_2026-08-28_raw.csv`
- `atlas_sample-flow_2026-08-28_draft.qmd`

Use ISO dates, stable separators and documented controlled vocabulary. Avoid names such as `final`, `final2`, `new`, `latest` or initials whose meaning is known only to one person. Do not place participant names or sensitive attributes in filenames.

When a version-control system manages text or code, use meaningful filenames plus commits and releases instead of manually duplicating every version.

## Make the data-management plan operational

The plan should answer:

- What will exist and why?
- Who owns, controls or has authority over it?
- Where may it be collected, transferred, processed and stored?
- Which formats, identifiers, metadata and standards apply?
- Who can access each state and how is that reviewed?
- How are integrity, confidentiality and availability protected?
- What is backed up, how often, where, for how long and by whom?
- How is restoration tested?
- What can be shared, under which licence, consent and governance conditions?
- What must be retained, archived, returned or destroyed, and when?
- What happens at role change, collaboration end or project closure?

ARDC good-data guidance covers planning, organisation, documentation, storage, access, sharing, publication and preservation [@ardc-good-data]. It is useful Australian infrastructure guidance, but institutional and project-specific requirements govern the actual system.

## Worked example: “everything is in Dropbox”

**Claim:** the project is safe because the folder synchronises to three laptops.

**Audit finds:** raw identifiable interviews, the re-identification key and public presentation files share one folder; everyone has edit access; a departed assistant still has access; local disks are unencrypted; deleted files are recoverable only for an unknown period; and no restore has been tested.

**Redesign:** move identifiable data and the separately protected key into approved controlled locations; remove unnecessary local copies; establish role-based access and offboarding; keep non-sensitive code and documentation in the collaboration space; verify the institutional backup service; conduct a restore into a safe test location; record recovery time, completeness and permissions; schedule quarterly access and restore reviews.

Three synchronised vulnerabilities are not three backups.

## Test restoration, not merely backup creation

Choose a representative and a difficult recovery scenario:

- accidental deletion;
- corrupted file discovered after several versions;
- lost or replaced device;
- departed account owner;
- unavailable collaborator or service;
- encryption key or credential recovery; or
- full project handover.

For the test record:

- what was selected and why;
- backup source and date;
- person performing the restore;
- target test location;
- time to recovery;
- integrity comparison, such as checksum, row count, file manifest or known output;
- whether permissions and metadata survived;
- failures and corrective action; and
- next test date.

Never restore sensitive data into an unapproved test location.

## Plan for retention, disposal and handover

Do not invent a universal retention period. Determine requirements from current institutional policy, legislation, ethics approval, funder, contract, discipline, community governance and publication commitments.

At closure decide, with authority:

- which records form the retained research record;
- which identifiers or keys remain necessary;
- what moves to an archive or repository;
- licences, access conditions and metadata;
- what must be returned or destroyed;
- how destruction is verified across active, synced and backup copies where required;
- who becomes custodian; and
- how future correction or reuse can be supported.

The Australian Code requires clear, accurate, secure and complete research records [@australian-code-2018]. A final clean dataset without the decisions and provenance needed to understand it may not meet that purpose.

## Storage arrangements that look safer than they are

- storing the only copy on a laptop, portable drive or departing account;
- treating sync, version history and backup as identical;
- putting identifiers, contact details and working data together;
- giving the whole team permanent edit access;
- using filenames as the only provenance record;
- changing raw data in place;
- encrypting data without a recoverable key process;
- assuming an approved service authorises every data type or transfer;
- scheduling backups without restore tests;
- promising deletion or long-term sharing the system cannot deliver.

## When the data system is recoverable

Before collection or restricted-data access:

- every material class is inventoried;
- the authoritative copy and custodian are known;
- locations and transfers are approved;
- access is role-based and reviewable;
- raw and identifying material are protected from accidental overwrite or release;
- folder, naming, metadata and version rules are documented;
- backup coverage and retention are verified;
- one realistic restore has passed; and
- retention, disposal, archive and handover decisions have identified authorities.

## Show the data steward the real storage map

Bring:

- the [living data-management plan](../../templates/data-management-plan.qmd);
- the complete data-flow and location map;
- sensitivity and authority classification;
- current access register;
- backup-service evidence and last restore result;
- expected volume, formats and collaboration pattern;
- retention, disposal and handover constraints; and
- one precise unresolved authority, security or recovery question.
